body_paragraphs: Twelve games is a long time to lose in any sport, and it ended the way these things sometimes do - not from resolve but from someone else's mistake. Philadelphia's closer walked in the tying run Tuesday and then gave up the winner, and Miami had its first win since July 9: Griffin Conine's single settling a streak that had become the whole season's story. The Marlins are 53-53 now, which sounds unremarkable until you remember where 52-53 came from three weeks ago.

Everything upstream of Miami kept moving too. Trump and Netanyahu met at the White House Tuesday for the first time since the Iran war began, calling it 'positive and productive' - agreement on the one thing (no Iranian nuclear weapon) that started this, if not yet on how it ends. Oil kept easing, Brent down another notch into the mid-to-high $80s, and the Fed's two-day meeting opened with Monday's premarket rally already fading into a mixed close. Wednesday at 2 PM decides the rest.

A quieter number from your own world: Waste Management just paid $379 million for a Medley landfill site, financing 96% of it through the seller rather than a bank - a more honest read on 2026 capital markets than any deal-volume statistic. And if you're near Virginia Key: Miami votes on Marine Stadium's fate on August 18, worth knowing what's actually on the ballot before you have an opinion on it.

themes.title: The streak ends at twelve, and it ends on an accident
themes.thesis: A record built on losing well enough to lose again broke the way losing streaks usually do - on someone else's mistake.
themes.synthesis: Miami beat the Phillies 8-7 Tuesday to end its franchise-record 12-game losing streak, its first win since July 9. Philadelphia closer Jhoan Duran entered with a two-run lead in the ninth but loaded the bases with no outs; Heriberto Hernandez tied it with a two-run single, and Griffin Conine walked it off with an RBI single. Hernandez and Conine had both already gone deep against Phillies ace Zack Wheeler, with Jakob Marsee and Otto Lopez each driving in a run.
themes.new_today: The win itself, and the specific way it happened - a blown ninth-inning lead by Philadelphia's closer rather than anything Miami's lineup solved on its own.
themes.why_it_matters: Twelve losses raised the real question - not whether Miami could win again, but what kind of team would be left when it did; a chaotic ninth doesn't answer that, but at least it stops the record from growing.

Brent crude kept easing alongside the diplomacy, down modestly Tuesday into the mid-to-high $80s, extending Monday's roughly 7% drop and remaining well off last week's near-$100 peak.

themes.title: A show about cities that keep rebuilding themselves opens at The Bass
themes.thesis: Cruzvillegas built a career treating precarity as material; here he turns that lens on the identities that get remade every time a city, or a life, is.

The Mexican conceptual artist built the work around the physical displacements common to diasporic communities, meant to make visitors newly aware of how their own identities keep re-forming as their surroundings do. themes.title: An old essay on insults, resurfaced this week, still holds up
themes.thesis: The Stoic case against taking offense easily was never really about manners - it's about who gets to set the terms of your peace of mind.
themes.synthesis: Donald Robertson's essay 'Stoicism, Insults, and Political Correctness' - written in response to William Irvine's writing on why insults hurt and shouldn't - argues the Stoics treated an insult as an event you interpret, not an injury inflicted on you directly; the offense lives in the judgment, not the words. Robertson frames it as a balance between indifference and genuine ethical concern, not a license to ignore real harm.
themes.new_today: Not a new essay - it dates to 2019 - but it was recirculated this week in a widely-read Stoicism newsletter's Sunday roundup, and its argument holds up unusually well against how the term gets used now.
themes.why_it_matters: Worth reading against your own week: distinguishing what's actually worth a reaction from what's just a judgment you're choosing to make is the same skill today's noticing prompt is asking for.

beautiful_thing.title: Miami Marine Stadium
beautiful_thing.creator: Hilario Candela, architect
beautiful_thing.body: Hilario Candela was 27 and newly arrived from Cuba when he designed this waterfront grandstand on Virginia Key - a cantilevered concrete roof folding out over 6,500 seats facing a basin built for powerboat racing, engineered so the whole structure seems to float free of its own supports. It closed after Hurricane Andrew in 1992 and has sat empty over the water for more than three decades since. The city has now begun partial pile and seating repairs with county and state grant money, and Miami voters decide its longer-term future - a proposed 40-year management deal with an arena operator - in a referendum scheduled for August 18.

daily_puzzle.prompt: A commodity opens the month at $100 a barrel. On each of the next five days, it falls by 10% of that day's starting price. On the sixth day, it rises by 50% of its new (post-decline) price. To the nearest dollar, what is the price at the end of day six?
daily_puzzle.hint: Percentages compound - each day's move applies to the previous day's new price, not the original $100.
daily_puzzle.explanation: Five straight 10% drops leave the price at 100 x 0.9^5 = $59.05. A 50% rise on that gives 59.05 x 1.5 = $88.57, which rounds to $89 - a reminder that a run of identical-sounding percentage moves compounds faster on the way down, and needs a bigger bounce than intuition suggests to fully reverse.
